Key Provisions of the Crapo-Cassidy Bill
The core of the Republican proposal centers on giving funds directly to patients rather than to insurance companies. 
•Health Savings Accounts (HSAs): The bill would redirect federal funds to health savings accounts for eligible individuals enrolled in bronze or catastrophic ACA plans.
•Direct Payments: Eligible individuals earning less than 700% of the federal poverty level would receive a one-time deposit into their HSA, varying by age.
◦$1,000 for individuals aged 18 to 49.
◦$1,500 for individuals aged 50 to 64.
•Usage of Funds: The money in the HSA could be used for out-of-pocket medical expenses like copays and deductibles, but not for monthly insurance premiums.
•Exclusions: The legislation includes language preventing the federal funds from being used for gender-affirming care or abortions.
•Medicaid Changes: It proposes reducing federal Medicaid funding to states that provide coverage to undocumented immigrants and adds requirements for states to verify citizenship status. 

Context and Expected Outcome
This bill is a counter-proposal to a Democratic bill that would extend the expiring enhanced ACA tax credits for three years. 
•Political Division: The Republican bill does not have Democratic support, and Democrats have called it "junk insurance".
•Expected Failure: Both the Republican and Democratic proposals lack the necessary bipartisan support to reach the 60 votes required to pass in the Senate, meaning both are expected to fail when they come to a vote. 
Without a legislative solution, the expiration of the current ACA subsidies will cause premiums to more than double for roughly 22 million Americans in 2026.
